title: Trends in global climate change
competency: Explain the global trends in climate change.

keywords.def: Things people do, such as burning fossil fuels and clearing forests, that change the climate (anthropogenic causes).
Clearing forests; it releases the CO₂ stored in trees and removes a sink.
Tiny liquid and solid particles in the air, from natural and human sources; most cool the surface.
Gases such as CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O that trap heat and raise air temperature near the ground (GHGs).
The increase, over many years, of the average temperature of the Earth.
Cutting the amount of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere.

en.text: Human activities such as deforestation and emissions from industry and transport add greenhouse gases and aerosols to the atmosphere. The IPCC Third Assessment Report (2001) found that the 1990s were the warmest decade and 1998 the warmest year since records began in 1861, that the twentieth century was likely the warmest of the last 1,000 years, and that most warming of the past 50 years came from human activities. Warming already affects sea level, snow cover, ice sheets and rainfall.

am.text: የ2001 የIPCC ሪፖርት፡ 1990ዎቹ በጣም ሞቃታማ አሥርት፣ 1998 በጣም ሞቃታማ ዓመት ነበሩ፤ ያለፉት 50 ዓመታት ሙቀት በአብዛኛው በሰው ምክንያት ነው።

screens.title: Your locality in 20 years
screens.ask: What do you expect in your locality over the next 10 or 20 years?
screens.after: The book expects temperatures to keep rising; rain may come in heavier spells with longer dry periods between.

screens.title: Natural and human changes
paras: The Earth's climate has always changed.
Some changes have natural causes.
Others come from human activities: deforestation, emissions from industry and transport.
These put gases and aerosols into the atmosphere.
The gases trap heat near the ground, like a greenhouse.
They are called greenhouse gases (GHGs).

screens.title: IPCC Third Assessment Report (2001)
paras: Observations show a warming world.
The 1990s: the warmest decade worldwide.
1998: the warmest year since records began in 1861.
The 20th century: likely the warmest in the last 1,000 years.
Most warming of the past 50 years: from human activities.
Warming already affects sea level, snow cover, ice sheets and rainfall.

ideas.name: How fast? Warming rates and projections

en.text: The average global surface temperature warmed 0.80 °C in the past century and 0.60 °C in the past three decades. That is 0.08 °C per decade over the century but 0.20 °C per decade recently, about 2.5 times faster. If greenhouse gas emissions keep rising, the IPCC (2001) projected a rise of 1.4 °C to 5.8 °C by the end of the 21st century.

Past three decades: +0.60 °C.

screens.ask: 0.80 °C of warming over 10 decades is ___ °C per decade
0.60 °C of warming in 3 decades is ___ °C per decade
screens.clue: Divide by the number of decades.

screens.ask: Recent warming (0.20 °C per decade) is ___ times the century rate (0.08 °C per decade)
screens.clue: Divide the bigger rate by the smaller.

screens.text: If GHG emissions keep rising, by how much did the IPCC (2001) project mean global temperature to rise by 2100?
screens.clue: A range of a few degrees.

notes.text: p.38: "They are known as greenhouse gases" follows "gases and aerosols"; aerosols are not GHGs (the book itself says most cool the surface, p.42–43). "Subsquently" is a typo.

Figure 2.3: the left graph has no y-axis scale (about −0.4 to +0.6 °C against 1951–1980 in the NASA original); the right panel is IPCC AR4 (2007), whose 1.1–6.4 °C range differs from the 1.4–5.8 °C (IPCC 2001) in the text.
Brainstorming Activity 2.2 is cut off ("increase or ..."); it should read "increase or decrease?". The unit outcome promises Ethiopian trends but the section gives only global data.
The rate-per-decade steps and blanks are added calculations from the book's numbers.
